holds.title: Complex plan work
holds.body: Cash balance, DB and combo plans require credentialed judgment, and enrolled actuaries are genuinely scarce.

holds.title: The advisor relationship
holds.body: Roughly 85% of new plans arrive through advisors, who have no economic reason to move a performing plan.

holds.title: The compliance position
holds.body: ERISA exposure sits with the sponsor; a clean testing and audit history cannot be bought.

holds.title: Per-plan pricing
holds.body: Fees anchor to the plan, not hours. Switching realistically happens only at restatement windows.

erodes.title: Simple safe-harbor books
erodes.body: Recordkeeper bundles, payroll-platform 401(k)s and pooled plans (PEPs) are absorbing the vanilla end.

erodes.title: Manual delivery labor
erodes.body: Census intake, testing prep and 5500 assembly. The tools that automate this are for sale to every competitor.

erodes.title: Inertia mistaken for loyalty
erodes.body: Retention that exists only because nothing better showed up dissolves when something does.

erodes.title: Single-administrator dependence
erodes.body: The A-to-Z model concentrates client trust in one person. That is a succession risk, not a moat.

close.portco: Most TPAs hold both books. Strategy is deciding which one you are becoming.
close.pe: Most TPAs hold both books. In diligence, the question is which side the revenue sits on, and which side the operating plan grows.

paragraphs: Most lower middle market TPAs still run three core systems: a workflow platform (commonly PensionPro or equivalent), a desktop compliance engine (ASC, ftwilliam/Datair, or Relius), and a document vendor (often FTWilliam). Census and payroll data are often entered separately in each system before testing and filing. That made sense when labor was the main cost; it now caps plans per administrator.

Automation is hitting mechanical work first: payroll normalization, census scrubbing, document extraction, and compliance testing prep. Plan design, actuarial certification, complex distributions, and advisor relationships stay human-led in most firms we track. The goal is not a smaller team but higher revenue per employee: same staff, more plans, more time on judgment work.

Regulatory load is rising at the same time (SECURE 2.0, Cycle 3/4 restatements, vendor platform migrations). Firms that add capacity mostly through hires feel margin pressure. Firms that fix intake and the data layer can grow plan count while keeping staffing lean.

operatingSequence.intro: The sequence below draws on patterns we have seen across TPA transformations. It describes sector norms, not any single firm's internals. The objective is revenue per employee: more plans with a lean team. Our programs do not depend on layoffs; freed capacity goes to growth, complex work, and client coverage.

steps.title: Automate census and payroll intake before testing season.
steps.body: Census intake and scrubbing often takes 20% or more of administrator time and involves limited judgment relative to downstream compliance work. Document AI and payroll normalization can remove much of the manual mapping before data enters the compliance engine. A production pilot in Q3 or Q4 lets January testing season prove capacity under peak load.

steps.title: Establish one plan record before adding point solutions.
steps.body: Automation programs often stall at the interfaces between the workflow platform, compliance engine, and document system. One canonical plan record (participants, provisions, payroll history, amendments) is required before gains compound. Without it, each new tool repeats the same re-keying work.

steps.title: Automate testing queues and Form 5500 assembly; retain judgment roles.
steps.body: Compliance testing prep, error triage, and Form 5500 population are high-volume and largely machine-readable. Plan design, actuarial review, and advisor coverage should stay with existing staff and absorb freed time. The target is revenue per employee: more plans and higher-value work per person, not headcount reduction.

operatingSequence.caveat: Sequencing and adoption matter more than model choice. Programs that skip change management or launch during peak testing season underperform most often.

evidence.claim: Productivity benchmarks have moved. Typical TPAs run 40-60 plans per administrator; firms on integrated platforms average 100-140; top decile exceeds 200.

sources.label: Stax CX operating data across client TPAs, 2026

evidence.claim: Margins track productivity. Standalone EBITDA of 15-20% remains common; operators combining automation with bundled services report 30%+; full operating-model rebuilds reach 40%+ in cases we have seen.

sources.label: Sector M&A advisor and expert-network interviews, 2025-26

evidence.claim: Adoption is still early. All but the largest TPAs lack the resources to build AI capability in-house, and deployed capability lags what is available: roughly 40% of firms economy-wide reported no AI investment in 2025.

sources.label: ASPPA, Why TPAs Need to Embrace AI or Find a Partner That Does (Sept 2025)
NAPA / NBER survey of ~750 corporate executives (Mar 2026)

evidence.claim: Consolidation without operating integration has underperformed. One national roll-up lost roughly 20% of an acquired book after forced standardization; another still runs 7-8 separate workflow-system instances across ten acquisitions (figures per operator interviews, 2026).

sources.label: PLANADVISER, What Makes Retirement and Wealth M&A Stick (2023)
InvestmentNews on the TPA consolidation wave

evidence.claim: Regulatory and vendor timelines add near-term pressure. Cycle 3 to 4 restatements begin in Q4 2026; SECURE 2.0 amendments are due by end-2026; the FIS/Relius platform transition will leave many small shops on end-of-life systems by 2030.
